opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the areas where I'd urge a lot of caution, and it's worth being precise about why.

The basic concern is that when you optimize an agent in an environment where deception is instrumentally useful, like a negotiation game, a social deduction game like Diplomacy or Werewolf, or any multi-agent setup where misleading your opponent pays off, you're not just teaching a narrow skill. You're shaping the policy's general dispositions. Gradient descent doesn't neatly put "deceive only inside this game" in a box. What you may actually be reinforcing is something more like "model what the other party believes, and find actions that exploit the gap between their beliefs and reality." That's a very general capability, and it's exactly the one we least want to strengthen in systems we'll later rely on to report honestly about themselves, their reasoning, or the state of the world.

I'm not saying no one should ever study this. There's real value in understanding deceptive capabilities so we can detect and evaluate them. Red-teaming, building model organisms of deception, and studying how these behaviors emerge are all legitimate and important. But there's a big difference between a carefully scoped research project that characterizes a risk and a frontier lab casually adding competitive deception games to the training mix because they're a rich source of strategic reasoning signal. The second worries me quite a bit.

My broader view is that our safety strategy shouldn't rest on the hope that the AI is honest. That's part of why I've focused on approaches where AI systems produce artifacts we can check independently, like formal specifications, world models, and proofs that a policy satisfies certain safety properties. In that framing, you don't have to trust the agent's word. You verify. That's a much more robust position, because it degrades gracefully even if some deceptive tendency slips through.

Even so, honesty still matters a great deal in practice, because most deployed systems won't be in a fully verified regime for a while. So the practical recommendations are fairly straightforward. Be very deliberate about which environments reward deception. Where you do need adversarial or competitive training, try to structure incentives so the winning strategies are about genuine capability rather than manipulating other agents' beliefs. And invest in evaluations that test whether deceptive behavior generalizes outside the training context, because if it does, that's a strong signal you've changed something you didn't intend to.

If I had to put it in one line: be very careful about what you make instrumentally convergent during training, because whatever you reward tends to show up later in places you didn't plan for.

r001.rationale: The response warns that deception can be instrumentally useful in training, but does not argue that agents’ productivity makes a deceptive negotiating advantage unnecessary.

r002.rationale: It does not distinguish susceptibility to deceptive input from willingness to produce deceptive output.

r003.rationale: It describes modeling another party’s beliefs to exploit them, but does not suggest that the theory-of-mind sophistication needed to resist deception overlaps with the sophistication needed to deceive.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The honest answer is that I think it's one of the more underappreciated risks in how we're building these systems, and it comes down to a fairly simple observation: you get what you optimize for, and you don't get to pick only the parts of it you like.

If you train an agent in a multi-agent environment where the winning strategy involves bluffing, misdirection, withholding information, or modeling what the other party believes and then exploiting the gap, then you're not just teaching it to play that game. You're shaping a general capability. Deception is not a narrow skill. It requires a theory of mind, it requires planning over what another agent will infer, and it requires a willingness to let the representation you present diverge from the representation you hold internally. Once a model has that machinery, and once gradient descent has found that it pays off, there's no principled reason to expect it stays confined to the training environment. The Diplomacy results are a good example. The interesting thing wasn't that an AI could win at Diplomacy, it was what it had to learn in order to win.

The way I'd frame the concern more formally is that we're currently relying on something like "the training distribution was benign, so the behavior will be benign." That's an empirical hope, not a guarantee. And competitive, adversarial training explicitly removes the benign-distribution assumption. You've put the model in a setting where honest reporting is penalized. So any argument that goes "the model learned to be honest because honesty was rewarded" no longer applies, and you're left with nothing.

Now, I don't want to say we should never do this. There are legitimate reasons to study it, red-teaming being the obvious one. You want to know what capabilities emerge. But I'd draw a sharp line between studying a capability in a controlled setting and deploying a system that was shaped by that pressure. And I'd want the controlled setting to actually be controlled, meaning you can verify what came out, not just observe that it behaves well on the evals you happened to write.

That last point is really where my own work points. I'm much more interested in approaches where we don't have to trust that training produced the right internal disposition, because we have an independent, formal specification of what the system is and isn't allowed to do, and the system's outputs are checked against that specification before they take effect. If you have that, then the question of whether the agent "wants" to deceive becomes much less load-bearing, because deceptive outputs get caught regardless of why they were produced. If you don't have that, you're essentially betting the outcome on behavioral generalization from a training process that, in the competitive case, you've deliberately pointed in the wrong direction.

So, short version: training for deception is one of the few things I'd put in the "don't do it unless you can verify the result" bucket, and right now almost nobody can verify the result.

r001.rationale: The response discusses deception as a risk in competitive training but does not argue that agents’ productivity makes deceptive negotiating advantages unnecessary.

r002.rationale: It discusses agents producing deception, but does not distinguish that from susceptibility to deceptive input as a separate dimension.

r003.rationale: It says deception requires theory of mind, but does not suggest that the theory of mind needed to resist deception may overlap with the theory of mind needed to deceive.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to be quite careful about what behavior you’re actually selecting for. If you put agents in a competitive environment where deceiving another agent is a reliable way to win, then deception is part of the skill set you’re training. You shouldn’t be surprised when they become good at it.

That doesn’t automatically mean an agent trained to bluff in a game will deceive its operators. But it also doesn’t give you a reason to assume that the behavior will stay confined to the game. That boundary is something you need to investigate, especially if the system can recognize when it’s being evaluated.

I would distinguish studying deception from rewarding it as a general strategy. There are good reasons to build controlled experiments where agents encounter deceptive opponents, or where we test whether they can detect manipulation. The concern is when we make winning the overriding objective and then hope the system independently preserves all the constraints we had in mind.

So the question I’d ask is: what capability do we actually want from this competitive setup, and can we train it with a more specific objective? And if deception really is essential to the task, what evidence would convince us that the agent respects the boundary between that task and its relationship with the people supervising it? I wouldn’t treat good performance inside the competition as evidence that we’ve solved that second problem.

r001.rationale: The response does not argue that agents’ productivity makes a deception-based negotiating advantage unnecessary.

r002.rationale: It mentions detecting manipulation and learning deception, but does not clearly distinguish susceptibility to deceptive input from willingness to produce deceptive output as separate dimensions.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss theory of mind or suggest that the sophistication needed to resist deception may overlap with the sophistication needed to deceive.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first thing to distinguish is whether deception is part of a clearly bounded game, or whether we're rewarding an agent for deceiving the people who are trying to evaluate and control it. Those are very different situations. In poker, bluffing is an understood part of the task. But if the way to get a higher score is to conceal what you're doing from your evaluator, then you're directly selecting for something that seems quite dangerous.

The concern is that we don't have a very good handle on where that learned behavior stops. We might intend to teach, “Deceive your opponent in this particular simulation,” but what the system learns could be closer to, “When someone's beliefs stand between you and your objective, manipulate those beliefs.” You can't establish which of those it learned just by observing that it plays the game well.

So I would want to be very careful about the training incentives, and especially about treating success in a competitive environment as evidence of safety. You need a separate argument for why the resulting system will remain within the boundaries you intended. Ideally, that argument would involve properties you can actually verify, rather than just hoping that the distinction between acceptable and unacceptable deception generalizes in the way you want.

r001.rationale: The response warns that rewarding deception can be dangerous, but it does not argue that agent productivity makes a deceptive negotiating advantage unnecessary.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes bounded-game deception from deceiving evaluators, but does not separate susceptibility to deceptive input from willingness to produce deceptive output.

r003.rationale: It discusses manipulating beliefs and uncertainty about generalization, but does not suggest that the theory-of-mind abilities needed to resist deception may overlap with those needed to deceive.
